_comment: Powers the Glossary & Sources reference page. Grouped by theme for browsability; the widget also supports free-text search across all groups.

terms.definition: One key does both jobs: locking and unlocking. Fast, but that single key is a single point of failure — anyone who gets it reads everything it protects.
Two mathematically linked keys: a public one that only locks, and a private one that only unlocks. Slower than symmetric, but solves the problem of handing out keys safely.

Using both at once: a fast symmetric key encrypts the actual data, then a slower asymmetric key encrypts ("wraps") that symmetric key. Gets the speed of one approach and the safety of the other — this is how virtually all ransomware, and most real-world encryption, actually works.
The industry-standard symmetric cipher, fast enough to encrypt an entire hard drive in minutes. Formally defined by NIST in FIPS 197.
A widely used asymmetric (public-key) algorithm, named after its inventors Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman. Formally defined by NIST in FIPS 186-5.
A newer family of asymmetric algorithms that reaches the same security level as RSA with much smaller keys, by doing math on points along a curve instead of huge prime numbers.
One specific, widely trusted elliptic curve used for fast, secure key exchange.

A way for two sides to agree on a shared secret key without ever sending that key across the network — each side combines its own private key with the other's public key and lands on the same result independently. This is how a ransomware sample and its operators can derive the same wrapping key without the key itself ever being transmitted.

A key generated fresh for a single use — one file, one session — then discarded rather than reused. If an ephemeral key were ever recovered, it wouldn't expose anything encrypted before or after it, unlike a long-term key shared across many operations.

A fast stream cipher, a variant of ChaCha20, commonly used for the bulk data-encryption step in a hybrid scheme. The "X" means it uses a longer, safely-random nonce, making accidental nonce reuse — the mistake that has broken weaker ransomware — much harder.

Encryption that also proves the ciphertext hasn't been tampered with, not just that it's unreadable. Poly1305 is a widely used algorithm for generating that tamper-detection tag, often paired with ChaCha20-family ciphers.

A well-regarded cryptography library (pronounced "salt") built to make strong primitives hard to misuse. Its crypto_box function bundles key exchange, encryption, and tamper-detection into one call — popular with ransomware authors for the same reason it's popular everywhere else: it's harder to get wrong than assembling the pieces by hand.
Data after encryption — unreadable without the right key.
Data before encryption, or after successful decryption — the readable original.
A public key and private key generated together, mathematically linked, used in asymmetric encryption.

A number used once, mixed into an encryption operation so encrypting the same data twice never produces the same ciphertext twice. Reusing one with certain ciphers is a serious implementation bug — one of the real ways ransomware encryption has been broken.

A program that generates numbers that look random. If it's seeded predictably — like from the system clock — an attacker who knows roughly when it ran can sometimes guess the numbers it produced, including encryption keys.
A one-way fingerprint of data: the same input always produces the same short output, but the output can't be reversed back into the input. Used to verify a file hasn't changed, among other things.
The first few bytes of a file, which identify its true type to the operating system — independent of whatever the filename or extension claims.

A measure, on a scale of 0.0 to 8.0, of how unpredictable a sequence of bytes is. Named for Claude Shannon, who defined it mathematically in 1948. Encrypted data reads close to 8.0, because looking indistinguishable from random noise is the whole design goal of encryption, not a side effect.
Windows' built-in cryptographic libraries. CNG, accessed via Bcrypt.dll, is the modern replacement for the older CryptoAPI (Advapi32.dll).

A Windows mechanism that lets a small pool of threads efficiently handle a large number of simultaneous file or network operations. Legitimate high-performance software uses it too — it's also how ransomware achieves very high encryption throughput.

Windows' built-in snapshot system, used for File History and System Restore. Deleting these snapshots is one of the first things most ransomware does, since they're otherwise a free, immediate recovery path.
Security software that watches for suspicious behavior on a device in real time, rather than only matching known malware signatures.

Installing a legitimately signed but flawed driver on purpose, then exploiting its flaw to run code at the highest privilege level (kernel mode) — often specifically to kill EDR software that would otherwise resist being shut down normally.
The Windows prompt that asks "Do you want to allow this app to make changes to your device?" before granting administrator rights to a program.

A specific permission — like "back up any file, ignoring normal access rules" — attached to a running process. Windows processes carry a list of these; malware that gains admin rights often turns on extra ones beyond what it started with.
Windows' central hierarchical database of configuration settings — everything from installed software to, in ransomware's case, which icon Explorer shows for a given file extension.
NTFS's master index of every file on a drive: name, size, and — crucially for investigators — timestamps for creation, modification, and renaming.
A running log NTFS keeps of every change made to files on a volume, more granular than MFT timestamps alone.
NTFS's own internal transaction log, used to make the filesystem crash-safe. Also a rich source of fine-grained timeline evidence for investigators.
Code that checks the system's language or location settings and changes behavior based on the result. In ransomware, usually used to avoid encrypting machines in the operators' home region.
A business model where a core group builds and maintains the ransomware, and independent "affiliates" rent it to run their own attacks, splitting the profit.

Stealing a copy of the victim's data before encrypting it, then threatening to publish it — a second point of leverage that doesn't depend on whether the victim's backups let them recover without paying.
The standard way security researchers describe attacker behavior — broad goal, general method, specific implementation — so a behavior can be recognized even when the exact tool changes.
A specific, observable artifact — a file hash, an IP address, a registry key — that suggests a particular attack occurred.

A free, widely used knowledge base that catalogs real-world attacker behavior into a shared vocabulary. Each behavior gets a technique ID like T1486, so defenders across different tools and companies can describe the same thing the same way. Used throughout Modules 3 and 4 of this guide.

Malware that spreads itself to other machines on a network without further action from an operator — using stolen credentials, admin tools, or both to copy itself outward from an initial foothold. A ransomware encryptor with this feature turns one compromised machine into an entire-network incident on its own.

Moving from one compromised machine to another inside the same network, typically using tools that are normally legitimate — remote administration utilities, scheduled tasks, remote scripting — rather than a fresh exploit each time.
A public catalog of individually identified software vulnerabilities, each with an ID like CVE-2024-51324.

Microsoft's convention for labeling a financially motivated or otherwise not-yet-fully-attributed threat actor cluster with a temporary "Storm-" plus a number, before or instead of giving it a proper name. Storm-2697 in Module 4 is one example.
